question: A 23-year-old gravida-1-para-1 (G1P1) presents to the emergency department with fever, malaise, nausea, and abdominal pain. She says her symptoms started 2 days ago with a fever and nausea, which have progressively worsened. 2 hours ago, she started having severe lower abdominal pain that is diffusely localized. Her past medical history is unremarkable. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She has had 3 sexual partners in the past month and uses oral contraception. The vital signs include temperature 38.8°C (102.0°F) and blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg. On physical examination, the lower abdomen is severely tender to palpation with guarding. Uterine and adnexal tenderness is also elicited. A urine pregnancy test is negative. On speculum examination, the cervix is inflamed with positive cervical motion tenderness and the presence of a scant yellow-white purulent discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Inflammation of the cervix with positive cervical motion tenderness and purulent discharge -> Likely cervicitis -> 80% CHAIN: Severe lower abdominal pain with guarding and adnexal tenderness -> Suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) -> 70% CHAIN: Fever, malaise, nausea, and abdominal pain with a negative urine pregnancy test -> Less likely to be a ruptured ectopic pregnancy -> 60% CHAIN: Multiple sexual partners and oral contraception use -> Increased risk for sexually transmitted infections leading to PID -> 75% CHAIN: Onset of symptoms 2 days ago with worsening fever and nausea -> Progressive nature of symptoms points towards an infectious etiology like PID -> 80%
analysis: The patient's presentation with fever, malaise, nausea, abdominal pain, lower abdominal tenderness, uterine and adnexal tenderness, inflamed cervix with purulent discharge, and multiple sexual partners is highly suggestive of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). PID is commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The presence of cervical motion tenderness and purulent discharge further supports this diagnosis.
